subject: music
title: Disco (c. 1973–1979/80): four-on-the-floor, Studio 54, and the dance floor that became an industry
dek: In the early 1970s DJs in New York gay clubs extended soul and funk breaks into seamless sets. Producers layered strings over four-on-the-floor drums. The 12-inch single arrived. Giorgio Moroder and Donna Summer made "I Feel Love" with a synthesiser in Munich in 1977. Studio 54 opened the same year and became the era's public image. In 1979 a Chicago radio DJ blew up disco records in a baseball stadium and the genre collapsed commercially overnight. By 1980 disco was industry poison, but its infrastructure—the DJ, the 12-inch, the beat—became house, techno, and modern dance music.

thumb.alt: Studio 54 nightclub exterior entrance in New York City.

hero.alt: Studio 54 nightclub entrance on West 54th Street in Manhattan, with the club's iconic signage.
hero.caption: Studio 54, 254 West 54th Street, Manhattan, photographed in 2006. The nightclub opened on 26 April 1977 and became the public face of disco: celebrity guests, velvet ropes, selective door policy, and spectacle. Co-owners Steve Rubell and Ian Schrager ran the club until their 1979 arrests for tax evasion. Studio 54 represented disco's commercial peak and its distance from the underground gay and Black clubs where the music had originated. The building, originally the Gallo Opera House (1927), now houses the Roundabout Theatre Company.
hero.credit: David Shankbone / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0

honesty: Disco-era photographs of club interiors, DJs, and performers from 1973–1979 are mostly in commercial archives or private collections under copyright. Many iconic images—Studio 54 crowds, Paradise Garage dance floors, artist portraits—cannot be freely licensed. This lesson uses street and building photographs, equipment images, and a few public-domain or clearly free-license visuals, all captioned as what they are: places and objects, not portraits. Where a free-license portrait could not be verified, the lesson does without. All YouTube links point to official or Topic uploads; when official audio is unavailable the note explains what the link is. No AI images of people. No invented facts, quotes, or numbers.

timeline.label: Soul, funk, Philly sound, and the dance break
timeline.detail: Late 1960s and early 1970s: soul and funk records—James Brown, Sly and the Family Stone, Isaac Hayes—have instrumental breaks dancers respond to. In Philadelphia, producers Kenny Gamble, Leon Huff, and Thom Bell develop the Philadelphia soul sound: lush strings, horns, four-on-the-floor kick drums. In New York, DJs at gay clubs like the Loft (David Mancuso, opened 1970) and the Sanctuary play soul, funk, and Philly records in extended sets, blending tracks seamlessly. The DJ becomes a curator, not just a jukebox. European producers experiment with electronic dance music: Giorgio Moroder in Munich, the Munich machine sound.

timeline.label: The term "disco" and early records
timeline.detail: "Disco" as shorthand for discotheque—a French word for a club where recorded music is played—enters American music press. MFSB (house band for Philadelphia International Records) releases "TSOP (The Sound of Philadelphia)" in March 1973, used as the Soul Train theme. The record layers strings and horns over a steady four-on-the-floor beat. It reaches number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in April 1974. Other early disco-leaning records: Barry White's "Love's Theme" (1973), Eddie Kendricks's "Keep On Truckin'" (1973). These are not yet called disco by the artists; the label comes from the clubs playing them.

timeline.label: The 12-inch single and DJ culture expands
timeline.detail: In 1974 Tom Moulton, a producer and remixer, requests that a track be pressed on a 12-inch vinyl at 45 RPM instead of the standard 7-inch at 45 or 33⅓. The wider grooves allow louder volume and deeper bass, crucial for club sound systems. The 12-inch single becomes the disco format. Moulton pioneers the extended remix, stretching a three-minute single into a six- or eight-minute club version. More clubs open: the Gallery (Nicky Siano, 1973), 12 West (1974). The Paradise Garage (Larry Levan, DJ) does not open until 1977 but becomes the decade's most influential DJ residency.

timeline.label: Donna Summer, Giorgio Moroder, and synthesised disco
timeline.detail: Donna Summer, a Boston-born singer working in Munich, meets Italian producer Giorgio Moroder. In 1975 they release "Love to Love You Baby," a 17-minute track with breathy vocals, synthesisers, and a steady beat. Casablanca Records releases it in the US; it reaches number two on the Billboard Hot 100. In 1976 Summer and Moroder release "I Feel Love" (from the album I Remember Yesterday, 1977). The track is entirely synthesised: Moog modular synthesiser bass line, no live instruments except drums. It becomes a blueprint for electronic dance music. Brian Eno later says it marks a divide: before "I Feel Love" and after.

timeline.label: Studio 54 opens
timeline.detail: Steve Rubell and Ian Schrager open Studio 54 at 254 West 54th Street, Manhattan, in a former opera house and CBS television studio. The club's door policy is notoriously selective: celebrities, models, artists, and dancers are admitted; others wait in line. The interior has theatrical lighting, a DJ booth, balconies, and a dance floor under a crescent moon and spoon set piece (a cocaine reference). Studio 54 becomes the public image of disco: glamour, hedonism, celebrity, drugs. The club's fame overshadows the underground gay and Black clubs where disco originated. Rubell and Schrager are arrested for tax evasion in 1979; the club closes in 1980.

timeline.label: Saturday Night Fever and the Bee Gees commercial peak
timeline.detail: On 14 December 1977 the film Saturday Night Fever, directed by John Badham and starring John Travolta, is released. The soundtrack, featuring the Bee Gees ("Stayin' Alive," "Night Fever," "How Deep Is Your Love"), becomes the best-selling soundtrack of all time. The album sells over 40 million copies. Disco moves from clubs into shopping malls, radio playlists, and suburban living rooms. The Bee Gees, Australian brothers who had been pop and soft-rock artists, become the commercial face of disco. Critics and rock fans begin to resent disco as overproduced, shallow, and inescapable.

timeline.label: Disco Demolition Night, Comiskey Park
timeline.detail: Steve Dahl, a Chicago rock DJ fired when his station switched to a disco format, organises Disco Demolition Night at Comiskey Park between games of a White Sox doubleheader. Fans bring disco records; Dahl blows them up in centre field. The crowd storms the field, tears up the turf, and starts fires. The second game is forfeited. The event is widely seen as a backlash against disco, tinged with homophobia, racism, and resentment of the genre's association with gay, Black, and Latin audiences. After Demolition Night, radio stations drop disco; record labels cancel contracts. By late 1979 disco is commercially toxic.

timeline.label: The commercial collapse and Studio 54 closes
timeline.detail: In February 1980 Steve Rubell and Ian Schrager are sentenced to prison for tax evasion. Studio 54 closes. Disco record sales plummet. Major labels stop signing disco acts. Radio formats shift to rock, new wave, and adult contemporary. Many disco artists cannot get records released. The genre's name becomes a marketing liability; some records are relabeled as "dance" or "R&B." But the infrastructure remains: the DJ, the 12-inch, the four-on-the-floor beat, the synthesiser, the dance floor, the club. In Chicago, New York, and Detroit, DJs and producers take disco's tools and build house and techno.

fun_fact.title: Disco Demolition Night was a stadium forfeit and a cultural turning point
fun_fact.text: On 12 July 1979, between games of a Chicago White Sox doubleheader at Comiskey Park, rock DJ Steve Dahl detonated a crate of disco records in centre field. Fans who brought disco records were admitted for 98 cents. The explosion left a crater; the crowd stormed the field, tore up the turf, and started fires. The second game was forfeited to the Detroit Tigers, one of only a handful of forfeits in Major League Baseball history. The event was widely interpreted as a backlash against disco's association with gay, Black, and Latin communities—a rejection not just of the music but of the culture. After Demolition Night, radio stations across the US dropped disco. Record labels cancelled contracts. Many disco artists could not release records. The genre's commercial collapse was swift. But the tools—the DJ, the 12-inch, the synthesiser, the beat—survived and became house, techno, and modern dance music.

sections.title: Soul breaks, Philly strings, and the Loft: when DJs became curators

blocks.text: In the late 1960s dancers at nightclubs responded to the breaks in soul and funk records: the moments when the vocals dropped out and the rhythm section took over. James Brown's "Funky Drummer" (1970), Isaac Hayes's instrumental work on the Shaft soundtrack (1971), Sly and the Family Stone's groove-heavy tracks—these were dance-floor fuel. DJs noticed. At gay clubs in New York, where the clientele wanted to dance all night, DJs began blending records seamlessly, using two turntables and a mixer to avoid dead air. The DJ was not just playing hits. The DJ was building a set, a journey, a flow. This was curation.

David Mancuso opened the Loft, a private party in his Manhattan loft apartment, on Valentine's Day 1970. Admission was by invitation or membership; there was no liquor license, no velvet rope, no commercial pressure. Mancuso played soul, funk, and obscure imports on a high-fidelity sound system he had built himself. The Loft was not a disco yet—the word had not settled into music vocabulary—but it was a template: a DJ, a sound system, a dance floor, and an audience that trusted the DJ's taste. Other underground clubs followed: the Sanctuary (1969–1972), where Francis Grasso pioneered beatmatching and slip-cueing; the Gallery, opened by Nicky Siano in 1973. These were predominantly gay clubs, and they were the disco's origin.

In Philadelphia, producers Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff ran Philadelphia International Records and developed the Philly soul sound: lush orchestration, strings arranged by Thom Bell and Bobby Martin, four-on-the-floor kick drums, and warm bass lines. MFSB (Mother Father Sister Brother), the label's house band, released "TSOP (The Sound of Philadelphia)" in March 1973. The record became the Soul Train theme and reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in April 1974. The Philly sound was not yet disco, but it had the elements: steady pulse, strings, horns, a beat you could dance to for minutes without a break. This was the material DJs in New York were playing, and it was beginning to be called disco.

In Munich, Italy-born producer Giorgio Moroder was experimenting with electronic instruments. Moroder had worked as a songwriter and producer in Germany and had started using synthesisers—Moog modular systems—to create bass lines and textures that could not be played on traditional instruments. He met Donna Summer, a Boston-born singer who had moved to Munich to perform in the German production of Hair. In 1975 they recorded "Love to Love You Baby," a 17-minute track with breathy vocals and a hypnotic synthesiser groove. Casablanca Records released it in the US; it reached number two. This was disco as a studio construction, not a live band performance. It was also the first hint of what synthesisers could do to the dance floor.

sections.title: 1974–1977: the 12-inch single, "I Feel Love," and the night the studio opened

blocks.text: In 1974 Tom Moulton, a producer and remixer working in New York, asked a mastering engineer to cut a track on a 12-inch vinyl record at 45 RPM instead of the standard 7-inch 45 or 33⅓ LP format. The wider grooves on a 12-inch allowed the music to be cut louder and with more bass, which meant the record could fill a club without distortion. The format also allowed longer tracks—six, eight, ten minutes—without the compromises of an LP side. The 12-inch single became the disco format. DJs could play an entire track without interruption; dancers did not have to stop. Moulton pioneered the extended remix, taking a radio-length single and stretching it into a club version with longer instrumental sections, breakdowns, and builds. This was not just re-editing. It was re-composition for the dance floor.

On 15 May 1977 Donna Summer and Giorgio Moroder released the album I Remember Yesterday on Casablanca Records. One track, "I Feel Love," was unlike anything on radio. The bass line was a Moog modular synthesiser sequenced in a repetitive, mechanical pattern. The drums were electronic. The strings and pads were synthesised. Only Donna Summer's voice was human, and even her vocal was layered and processed. There were no guitars, no live bass, no horns. Brian Eno later said that when he heard "I Feel Love" he realised the future had arrived. The track reached number six on the Billboard Hot 100. It became a blueprint for electronic dance music: house, techno, trance, and every synthesised genre that followed. Producers stopped asking whether electronic instruments could replace live musicians. "I Feel Love" answered the question.

On 26 April 1977, five weeks before "I Feel Love" was released, Steve Rubell and Ian Schrager opened Studio 54 at 254 West 54th Street in Manhattan. The building had been the Gallo Opera House (1927), then a CBS television studio (Studio 52). Rubell and Schrager renovated the space: a large dance floor, theatrical lighting, balconies, a DJ booth, and a set piece with a crescent moon and a spoon lowering from the ceiling (widely interpreted as a cocaine reference). The door policy was selective. Marc Benecke, the doorman, stood outside and chose who entered based on appearance, celebrity, or whim. Celebrities—Andy Warhol, Liza Minnelli, Mick Jagger, Bianca Jagger (who famously rode a white horse into the club), Diana Ross—were admitted; others waited in line for hours and were turned away. Studio 54 was spectacle, exclusivity, hedonism, and fame. It was also disco's public face.

Studio 54 was not where disco started. The Loft, the Gallery, the Sanctuary, and later the Paradise Garage (opened 1977, DJ Larry Levan) were the underground rooms where the music and the culture were built. Studio 54 was where disco became a phenomenon, a tabloid story, a symbol of the 1970s. The press covered the club's celebrity guests and excesses. The door policy became infamous. Middle America learned about disco from Studio 54, not from the gay clubs where the genre had emerged. This distance between disco's origins and its public image would become a problem when the backlash arrived.

sections.title: Clubs, DJs, and the records that filled the floor

blocks.text: By 1977 disco had recognisable elements: four-on-the-floor kick drums (a steady kick on every quarter note), hi-hats marking the offbeats, a prominent bass line, orchestral strings or horns, and vocals that could be soulful, breathy, or chanted. The tempo was usually 110–130 beats per minute, fast enough to dance but not exhausting. The structure was simple: verse, chorus, instrumental breakdown, build, return to chorus. The breakdown—where the vocals dropped out and the rhythm section was isolated—was crucial. This was the moment when dancers responded, when the DJ could layer in another record, when the floor moved as a collective body.

The DJ was the architect. At the Paradise Garage, Larry Levan built sets that lasted hours, blending soul, funk, disco, and early electronic records with a mixing style that was both technical and emotional. Levan used the club's custom-built sound system—designed by Richard Long—to create a physical experience: the bass was not just heard but felt. Nicky Siano at the Gallery, Frankie Knuckles (who would later move to Chicago and help create house music), and David Mancuso at the Loft were also shaping the form. These DJs were artists. They selected tracks most people had never heard, extended them, layered them, and sequenced them into a narrative. The dance floor trusted them.

The records: Chic's "Le Freak" (1978), written by Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards after they were turned away from Studio 54, reached number one and sold six million copies. Chic's tight bass-and-guitar interlock—Rodgers on guitar, Edwards on bass—became a disco signature. Gloria Gaynor's "I Will Survive" (1978) became an anthem of resilience and a gay-club standard. Sylvester's "You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real)" (1978), performed by the openly gay Black falsetto singer from San Francisco, was a declaration of joy and liberation. Sister Sledge's "We Are Family" (1979), produced by Chic, was adopted as an anthem of unity. The Trammps' "Disco Inferno" (1976) became widely known after its inclusion in the Saturday Night Fever soundtrack. These records were not just hits. They were community texts, floor anthems, identity markers.

Disco was also lucrative. By 1978 disco records accounted for a significant portion of Billboard chart positions. Major labels signed disco acts. Session musicians and arrangers—like Gene Page, who arranged strings for Barry White, and Tom Moulton—were in constant demand. The 12-inch single became a profit centre. Clubs were packed. The business was growing. But the backlash was forming.

sections.title: Saturday Night Fever: the Bee Gees and disco's commercial peak

blocks.text: On 14 December 1977 Paramount Pictures released Saturday Night Fever, directed by John Badham and starring John Travolta as Tony Manero, a young man from Brooklyn who escapes his working-class life by dancing at a disco. The film's soundtrack, released by RSO Records, featured the Bee Gees—Barry, Robin, and Maurice Gibb—alongside other disco tracks. The Bee Gees contributed "Stayin' Alive," "Night Fever," "How Deep Is Your Love," and "More Than a Woman." The soundtrack became the best-selling album of all time until Michael Jackson's Thriller (1982). It sold over 40 million copies. It spent 24 weeks at number one on the Billboard 200.

The Bee Gees were not disco pioneers. They were Australian-British pop and soft-rock artists who had been recording since the 1960s. Their falsetto vocal harmonies and string-heavy production fit the disco format, and producer Arif Mardin helped them shape the sound for the film. "Stayin' Alive" became the era's anthem, played at weddings, proms, roller rinks, and shopping malls. The film and the soundtrack brought disco to Middle America. Suburban teenagers bought the album. Radio stations added disco to their playlists. Disco was no longer underground. It was inescapable.

Saturday Night Fever also changed how the public understood disco. The film presented disco as a working-class escape, a space where a young man could be exceptional through dance. This was not false, but it was partial. The film erased the gay clubs, the Black and Latin producers, the underground DJs. It turned disco into a story about a straight white man in Brooklyn. The film made disco commercially dominant, but it also made the genre vulnerable. When the backlash came, it would not spare Saturday Night Fever, but it would target the gay and Black artists who had built the form.

sections.title: Disco Demolition Night: the records exploded in a baseball stadium

blocks.text: Steve Dahl was a rock DJ at WDAI in Chicago. In December 1978 the station switched formats from rock to disco. Dahl was fired. He moved to WLUP, a rock station, and began an anti-disco campaign on air. He called himself a "disco sucks" advocate and played rock in defiance of disco's chart dominance. On 12 July 1979 Dahl and the Chicago White Sox organised Disco Demolition Night at Comiskey Park. The White Sox were playing a doubleheader against the Detroit Tigers. Between games, fans who brought a disco record would be admitted for 98 cents. Dahl would blow up the records in centre field.

Thousands of fans brought records. Dahl, dressed in military garb, detonated a crate of disco records between games. The explosion left a crater in the field. The crowd—estimated at over 50,000, far more than the stadium's capacity—stormed the field, tore up the turf, stole bases, and started fires. Security could not control the crowd. The second game was forfeited to the Tigers, one of only a handful of forfeits in Major League Baseball history. The images were broadcast nationally: thousands of mostly white, mostly male fans destroying disco records, chanting "disco sucks."

The event was widely seen as more than a music critique. Disco was associated with gay clubs, Black and Latin producers, and female vocalists. The "disco sucks" movement was tinged with homophobia, racism, and sexism. Rock fans resented disco's dominance on radio and charts. Disco represented something they rejected: softness, femininity, queerness, Blackness, electronic production over live instruments, dancing over guitar solos. Disco Demolition Night made that resentment visible. After the event, radio stations across the US dropped disco from their playlists. Record labels cancelled contracts. Disco became commercially toxic.

By the end of 1979 disco's commercial moment was over. Clubs were still operating, DJs were still working, but the record industry had abandoned the genre. In February 1980 Steve Rubell and Ian Schrager were convicted of tax evasion and sentenced to prison. Studio 54 closed. Disco records were no longer released under that name; they were relabeled as "dance," "R&B," or "urban contemporary." The genre that had dominated the charts for five years was suddenly a punchline. But the infrastructure did not die. The DJ, the 12-inch, the synthesiser, the four-on-the-floor beat—these tools moved underground, to Chicago and Detroit and New York, where they became house and techno.

sections.title: Munich, Jamaican dub, Black Rio, northern soul, and Tokyo's disco boom

blocks.text: In Munich, Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte were building what the press called the Munich sound or Eurodisco: synthesiser-driven, metronomic, electronic. Moroder produced not only Donna Summer but also other European disco acts. The Munich approach influenced producers across Europe and later became a foundation for Italo disco in the 1980s. In France, producer Alec R. Costandinos created orchestral disco with large string sections and dramatic arrangements. In the UK, producers like Biddu (who worked with Tina Charles) and Ian Levine (at northern soul clubs) were importing and producing disco records.

In Jamaica, disco's late 1970s peak coincided with the roots reggae and dub boom. Bob Marley and the Wailers, Peter Tosh, Burning Spear, and Culture were releasing albums on Island and other labels. Lee "Scratch" Perry and King Tubby were producing dub: instrumental remixes with heavy reverb, delay, and bass. Jamaican dub influenced disco remixers like Tom Moulton, who used similar techniques—extended instrumental sections, echo, dropping out elements to create space. Disco and dub were parallel studio experiments in dance-floor manipulation, though they served different audiences and venues.

In Rio de Janeiro, Black Rio was a movement of Black Brazilian musicians and dancers reclaiming soul, funk, and disco as Afro-Brazilian culture. DJ Big Boy (Newton Alvarenga Duarte) organised baile funk (funk balls) where thousands danced to American soul and disco imports. Brazilian artists like Tim Maia and Tony Tornado fused soul with samba and MPB (música popular brasileira). This was not disco imitation; it was Black Brazilian youth using the same tools—funk breaks, dance floors, sound systems—to assert identity in a society that marginalised them. The Black Rio movement peaked in the mid-to-late 1970s, contemporaneous with New York disco.

In the UK, northern soul—a subculture of working-class youth dancing to obscure American soul and Motown imports at all-night clubs in Northern England—overlapped with disco chronologically. Wigan Casino, the Twisted Wheel, and Blackpool Mecca were northern soul venues where rare 45s were prized and DJs like Ian Levine curated sets. Northern soul was not disco, but the culture was similar: DJ as curator, dance floor as community, American Black music as source material. By the late 1970s some northern soul DJs were incorporating disco records, especially Hi-NRG tracks with fast tempos. Hi-NRG—a synthesised, high-tempo disco offshoot—emerged in the UK and Europe in the late 1970s and early 1980s, after disco's US commercial collapse.

In Tokyo, disco clubs proliferated in the late 1970s. Shibuya and Roppongi neighbourhoods had clubs playing American and European disco imports. Japanese DJs adopted the same tools: two turntables, 12-inch singles, extended mixes. Japanese pop (kayōkyoku) absorbed disco's four-on-the-floor beat and string arrangements. Performers like Yamaguchi Momoe and Pink Lady incorporated disco elements into their records. Tokyo's disco scene was import-driven—American and European records, not Japanese production—but the dance floor culture was local. By 1980, when disco collapsed in the US, Tokyo's clubs were still operating, and Japanese producers were beginning to create their own electronic dance music in the 1980s.

sections.title: House, techno, and the tools that survived the backlash

blocks.text: Disco did not die. It went underground. In Chicago, Frankie Knuckles—who had been a DJ at the Gallery in New York—moved to the Warehouse club in 1977. When disco records became unavailable after 1979, Knuckles started editing and remixing tracks himself, using a Roland TR-808 drum machine and a reel-to-reel tape deck. He extended breaks, added electronic percussion, and layered samples. The music he played at the Warehouse became known as house music, named after the club. In 1984 Knuckles left the Warehouse; by then house was a recognized Chicago genre. Tracks like Jesse Saunders's "On and On" (1984) and Farley "Jackmaster" Funk's "Love Can't Turn Around" (1986) were early house records. House was disco's direct descendant: four-on-the-floor, 12-inch singles, DJ culture, synthesised production, and a predominantly gay and Black audience.

In Detroit, high school students Juan Atkins, Derrick May, and Kevin Saunderson were listening to Kraftwerk, Giorgio Moroder, and Parliament-Funkadelic on the radio. They were also listening to the Electrifying Mojo, a Detroit DJ who played an eclectic mix of electronic, funk, and new wave. In the early 1980s they began making their own tracks using synthesisers, drum machines, and sequencers. Atkins, working under the name Model 500, released "No UFO's" in 1985. Derrick May released "Nude Photo" (1987) and "Strings of Life" (1987). This was techno: machine-made, futuristic, repetitive, and hypnotic. Like house, techno was built on disco's infrastructure: the DJ, the 12-inch, the club, the synthesiser, the beat. But techno was colder, more abstract, more European in its references.

In New York, the Paradise Garage continued to operate until 1987. Larry Levan remained its resident DJ until it closed. The Garage's sound system and Levan's mixing style influenced a generation of producers and DJs. Garage house—a subgenre named after the club—emphasised soulful vocals and gospel-inflected piano over four-on-the-floor beats. Tracks like Loleatta Holloway's "Love Sensation" (1980) and Taana Gardner's "Heartbeat" (1981) were Garage anthems and later became house samples. By the mid-1980s disco's name was gone, but its tools were everywhere.

What survived the backlash was the method. The DJ as artist, not just a record player. The 12-inch single as a club format. The synthesiser as a lead instrument. Four-on-the-floor as the beat's foundation. The dance floor as a space of community, identity, and liberation. Disco as a genre was commercially dead by 1980, but disco as an infrastructure—the physical and cultural tools for making dance music—lived on in house, techno, garage, Hi-NRG, and every electronic dance genre that followed. Disco's erasure was political; its survival was structural. The backlash destroyed the industry, but the tools were too useful to abandon.

If disco was commercially destroyed in 1979–1980 by a backlash that was partly about music and partly about homophobia and racism, why did its tools—the DJ, the 12-inch, the synthesiser, the beat—survive and become the foundation of house, techno, and modern dance music? What does it mean for a genre to be culturally erased but structurally essential?

glossary.explain: Dance music genre c. 1973–1979/80, characterized by four-on-the-floor beats, orchestral arrangements, and extended club versions. Originated in gay clubs in New York.
French word for a nightclub where recorded music is played instead of live bands; shortened to "disco" in the US.
Drum pattern with a kick drum hit on every quarter note (beats 1, 2, 3, 4); foundational to disco, house, and techno.
Vinyl record format, 12 inches in diameter, pressed at 45 RPM for louder volume and deeper bass; disco's standard format.
DJ technique of matching the tempo of two records so they can be mixed seamlessly.
DJ technique of holding a record still while the platter spins beneath, then releasing it at the right moment to start the track on beat.
